The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ be a measurable parameter space and, for each integer $n\ge1$, let $\mathcal E_n=((\mathsf Y_n,\mathcal Y_n),(P_{\theta,n})_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a statistical experiment. Let $\Pi_{0,n}$ be a proper prior on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and let $y\mapsto\Pi_n(\cdot\mid y)$ be a supplied posterior probability kernel under the associated prior-predictive law. For $0<\gamma<1$, a data-indexed set rule $C_n:\mathsf Y_n\to\mathcal P(\Theta)$ is a posterior credible set at level $1-\gamma$ if its membership graph $\{(y,\theta):\theta\in C_n(y)\}$ is in $\mathcal Y_n\otimes\mathcal T$ and $\Pi_n(C_n(y)\mid y)\ge1-\gamma$ for every $y$ in its declared data domain. At a fixed truth $\theta\in\Theta$, its frequentist coverage is $c_n(\theta):=P_{\theta,n}\{y:\theta\in C_n(y)\}$. For a truth class $\mathcal T_n\subseteq\Theta$, the rule is asymptotically honest at level $1-\gamma$ on $\mathcal T_n$ if $\liminf_{n\to\infty}\inf_{\theta\in\mathcal T_n}c_n(\theta)\ge1-\gamma$, and it is asymptotically exactly calibrated there if $\sup_{\theta\in\mathcal T_n}|c_n(\theta)-(1-\gamma)|\to0$.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By The standard normal density has total mass one and The indefinite integral of a nonnegative measurable function is a measure, gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. The law of a random element is a probability measure makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in The Dirac set function at a point.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ (Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length,
Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

derivations.claim: Under [A1], the standard normal probability law of [F2] is supplied. Its density φ is positive and symmetric and integrates to one, so Φ is continuous and strictly increasing, with Φ(0)=1/2 and Φ(y)→1 as y→∞. Choose B>0 with Φ(B)>0.975. By [F3] on [0,B], there is a unique z>0 with Φ(z)=0.975.

The prior density times likelihood is proportional to $\exp\{-\tfrac12[\theta^2+(Y-\theta)^2]\}=\exp\{-(\theta-Y/2)^2\}$ times a factor independent of $\theta$. Normalization gives posterior law $N(Y/2,1/2)$.
Under the fixed truth $\theta_*=2r+1$, write $Y=\theta_*+Z$. The event $\theta_*\in I(Y)$ is equivalent to $|Z-\theta_*|\le2r$, hence to $1\le Z\le4r+1$.

The interval membership graph is $\{(Y,\theta):|\theta-Y/2|\le r\}$, the inverse image of the closed interval $[-r,r]$ under a continuous map. It is closed, hence Borel, so the sampling membership event is measurable.
Under that posterior, $(\theta-Y/2)/\sqrt{1/2}$ is standard normal. The interval radius $r=z/\sqrt2$ therefore gives posterior mass $\Phi(z)-\Phi(-z)=0.975-0.025=0.95$ for every observed $Y$.
Since the standard normal density is positive and symmetric, $P(1\le Z\le4r+1)<P(Z\ge0)=1/2<0.95$. Thus the interval has posterior mass $0.95$ but frequentist coverage below $0.95$ at $\theta_*$.

Write $\mathbb N_+=\{1,2,\ldots\}$. Let $\ell^2(\mathbb N_+,\mathbb R)$ be the real square-summable sequence space
from [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]. For $\beta>0$
and $M>0$, the **Gaussian-sequence hyperrectangle** of smoothness index
$\beta$ and radius $M$ is
$$\Theta_\beta(M):= \left\{\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N_+,\mathbb R): \sup_{i\ge1}i^{1+2\beta}\theta_i^2\le M\right\}.$$
The definition uses a coordinatewise weighted bound. It is distinct from the
Sobolev ellipsoid $\{\theta:\sum_i i^{2\beta}\theta_i^2\le M\}$.

Let $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ be the real square-summable sequence space
from [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]. Fix
$L_0\ge1$, an integer $N_0\ge1$, and $\rho\ge2$. The **polished-tail class**
$\Theta_{\mathrm{pt}}(L_0,N_0,\rho)$ consists of the sequences
$\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ such that for every integer
$N\ge N_0$,
$$\sum_{i=N}^{\infty}\theta_i^2 \le L_0\sum_{i=N}^{\lfloor\rho N\rfloor}\theta_i^2.$$
Thus each tail's total squared mass is controlled by the mass in the finite
block from $N$ through $\lfloor\rho N\rfloor$. The condition concerns block
energy; it is not a coordinatewise upper or lower bound.

The adaptive empirical-Bayes credible balls have nonvanishing frequentist
coverage uniformly over every truth in a hyperrectangle $\Theta_\beta(M)$.

**Explicit sparse-gap construction.**

Use [[def-adaptive-empirical-bayes-gaussian-sequence-procedure]], assume AC,
and fix $\beta>0$, $p\ge0$, $C\ge1$, $\gamma\in(0,1)$ and a finite
$A>\beta$. Run the procedure with the fixed cap $A_n=A$ and
$C^{-2}i^{-2p}\le\kappa_i^2\le C^2i^{-2p}$. Choose
$0<M\le(1984C^8)^{-1}$. Put $s=1+2\beta+2p$, $\rho_j=2^j$,
$n_1=2$, and
$$n_{j+1}=\left\lceil(2\rho_{j+1}^2)^s n_j\right\rceil,\qquad N_j=n_j^{1/s}.$$
Define the fixed nonnegative truth by
$$\theta_{0,i}^2=\begin{cases}0,&N_j/\rho_j<i\le N_j\text{ for some }j,\\0,&2N_j<i\le\rho_jN_j\text{ for some }j,\\Mi^{-1-2\beta},&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}$$
Then $\theta_{0,1}=0$ and $\theta_0\in\Theta_\beta(M)$. For every
deterministic nonnegative inflation sequence for which there exist
$K_L\in(0,\infty)$ and $j_0\in\mathbb N$ such that, for every $j\ge j_0$,
$$L_{n_j}\le K_L\sqrt M\,\rho_j^{(1+2p)/(8+8\beta+8p)}$$
one has
$$P_{\theta_0}^{(n_j)}\{\theta_0\in\widehat C_{n_j}(L_{n_j})\}\longrightarrow0.$$
The finitely many indices with $n_j<3$ are irrelevant. In particular,
for every $\beta>0$ this gives a counterexample for any fixed cap
$A>\beta$, including constant inflation factors.

Use the Gaussian sequence procedure of
[[def-adaptive-empirical-bayes-gaussian-sequence-procedure]] with fixed
$p\ge0$, $C\ge1$, $A>0$, and
$C^{-2}i^{-2p}\le\kappa_i^2\le C^2i^{-2p}$. Fix $L_0\ge1$, $N_0\ge1$,
$\rho\ge2$, and $\gamma\in(0,1)$. Assume that
$\theta_0\in\Theta_{\mathrm{pt}}(L_0,N_0,\rho)$ and
$\theta_{0,1}=0$. Then there is a finite inflation constant $L>0$,
depending only on the fixed model and class parameters, such that
$$\inf_{\substack{\theta_0\in\Theta_{\mathrm{pt}}(L_0,N_0,\rho)\\ \theta_{0,1}=0}} P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}\{\theta_0\in\widehat C_n(L)\} \longrightarrow1.$$
This is conservative frequentist coverage tending to one, not exact
asymptotic coverage $1-\gamma$. The source also allows a sequence of caps
$A_n>0$ satisfying, for all sufficiently large $n$,
$$A_n\le \frac{\sqrt{\log n}}{4\sqrt{\log(\rho\vee e)}}.$$
In that case there is a constant $K_{\mathrm{infl}}>0$, depending only on the
fixed model and class parameters and not on $n$, such that the same coverage
conclusion holds for any deterministic inflation sequence satisfying
$$L_n\ge K_{\mathrm{infl}}(3\rho^{3(1+2p)})^{A_n}$$
for all sufficiently large $n$.

Assume AC. Fix $n\ge3$, $p\ge0$, $C\ge1$, $\gamma\in(0,1)$,
an inflation factor $L\ge0$, and a finite $A_n>0$. Let
$(\kappa_i)_{i\ge1}$ be known nonzero real numbers satisfying
$$C^{-2}i^{-2p}\le\kappa_i^2\le C^2i^{-2p}.$$
For a true parameter $\theta_0\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, the observation
sequence is
$$X_i=\kappa_i\theta_{0,i}+n^{-1/2}Z_i,\qquad i\ge1,$$
where $(Z_i)_{i\ge1}$ are independent $N(0,1)$ random variables. The
corresponding sampling law is denoted $P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}$.

For $0<\alpha\le A_n$, let
$$\Pi_\alpha=\bigotimes_{i\ge1}N(0,i^{-1-2\alpha}).$$
Its coordinate posterior rule is the product of
$$N\!\left(\widehat\theta_{n,\alpha,i}(x), v_{n,\alpha,i}\right),\qquad \widehat\theta_{n,\alpha,i}(x)= \frac{n\kappa_i x_i}{i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2},\qquad v_{n,\alpha,i}=\frac{1}{i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2}.$$
For $\alpha>0$, the marginal log likelihood relative to the reference law
$\bigotimes_{i\ge1}N(0,n^{-1})$ is
$$\ell_n(\alpha;x)=-\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \left[ \log\!\left(1+\frac{n\kappa_i^2}{i^{1+2\alpha}}\right) -\frac{n^2\kappa_i^2x_i^2}{i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2} \right].$$
For maximization, use this same source score series at every
$\alpha\in[0,A_n]$, with the sum taken in increasing coordinate order.
Choose a Borel data domain $D_n\subseteq\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ such that
the series converges to a finite value for every $x\in D_n$ and every
$\alpha\in[0,A_n]$, and $\alpha\mapsto\ell_n(\alpha;x)$ is upper
semicontinuous there. For each truth under consideration assume
$P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}(D_n)=1$. Also assume a Borel-measurable selector
$x\mapsto\widehat\alpha_n(x)$ on $D_n$ is supplied, with
$\widehat\alpha_n(x)\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{0\le\alpha\le A_n}
\ell_n(\alpha;x)$.
These domain, endpoint-score and selector conditions are explicit procedure
hypotheses; no arbitrary score value at $\alpha=0$ is added. At
$\widehat\alpha_n>0$, let $r_{n,\gamma}(\widehat\alpha_n)$ be the
$1-\gamma$ quantile of the centered posterior $\ell^2$ norm and use the
posterior mean given above. Define the empirical-Bayes set by
$$\widehat C_n(L;x)= \begin{cases} \{\theta\in\ell^2: \|\theta-\widehat\theta_{n,\widehat\alpha_n(x)}(x)\|_2 \le Lr_{n,\gamma}(\widehat\alpha_n(x))\},& \widehat\alpha_n(x)>0,\\ \ell^2,&\widehat\alpha_n(x)=0. \end{cases}$$
Use the source convention $r_{n,\gamma}(0)=+\infty$ for the second branch;
no posterior probability on $\ell^2$ is asserted at $\alpha=0$. A separate
local lemma verifies the coordinate posterior and evidence formulas for
$\alpha>0$.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ be a measurable parameter space and, for each integer $n\ge1$, let $\mathcal E_n=((\mathsf Y_n,\mathcal Y_n),(P_{\theta,n})_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a statistical experiment. Let $\Pi_{0,n}$ be a proper prior on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and let $y\mapsto\Pi_n(\cdot\mid y)$ be a supplied posterior probability kernel under the associated prior-predictive law. For $0<\gamma<1$, a data-indexed set rule $C_n:\mathsf Y_n\to\mathcal P(\Theta)$ is a posterior credible set at level $1-\gamma$ if its membership graph $\{(y,\theta):\theta\in C_n(y)\}$ is in $\mathcal Y_n\otimes\mathcal T$ and $\Pi_n(C_n(y)\mid y)\ge1-\gamma$ for every $y$ in its declared data domain. At a fixed truth $\theta\in\Theta$, its frequentist coverage is $c_n(\theta):=P_{\theta,n}\{y:\theta\in C_n(y)\}$. For a truth class $\mathcal T_n\subseteq\Theta$, the rule is asymptotically honest at level $1-\gamma$ on $\mathcal T_n$ if $\liminf_{n\to\infty}\inf_{\theta\in\mathcal T_n}c_n(\theta)\ge1-\gamma$, and it is asymptotically exactly calibrated there if $\sup_{\theta\in\mathcal T_n}|c_n(\theta)-(1-\gamma)|\to0$.

derivations.claim: Every squared coordinate is either zero or $Mi^{-1-2\beta}$, so $\sup_i i^{1+2\beta}\theta_{0,i}^2\le M$ and $\sum_i\theta_{0,i}^2\le M\sum_i i^{-1-2\beta}<\infty$. Also $N_1=2^{1/s}\in(1,2)$ and $\rho_1=2$, hence $N_1/\rho_1<1\le N_1$ and the first zero gap contains $i=1$. Thus $\theta_0\in\Theta_\beta(M)$ and $\theta_{0,1}=0$.

Fix any polished-tail parameters $L_0\ge1$, integer $N_0\ge1$, and $\rho_*\ge2$. The recursion gives $N_j/\rho_j\ge2\rho_jN_{j-1}>\rho_{j-1}N_{j-1}$, so every earlier gap ends below $N_j/\rho_j$. Also $N'_j=\lfloor2N_j\rfloor+1\le2N_j+1$; because $N_j\to\infty$ and $\rho_j\to\infty$, for all sufficiently large $j$ we have $N'_j\ge N_0$ and $\rho_*(2N_j+1)\le\rho_jN_j$, whence $\lfloor\rho_*N'_j\rfloor\le\rho_jN_j$. Since $N'_j>2N_j$, the block $[N'_j,\lfloor\rho_*N'_j\rfloor]$ lies in the current zero gap $(2N_j,\rho_jN_j]$. For all sufficiently large $j$, $i_j=\lfloor\rho_jN_j\rfloor+1\le\rho_jN_j+1<4\rho_jN_j\le N_{j+1}/\rho_{j+1}$, so $i_j$ is before the next first gap; applying the same separation at later indices puts all still later gaps farther right. Since $\rho_jN_j>2N_j+1\ge N'_j$ eventually, $i_j>N'_j$; earlier gaps end below $N_j/\rho_j<i_j$. Hence $i_j$ lies outside every zero gap and is in the tail from $N'_j$, with $\theta_{0,i_j}^2=Mi_j^{-1-2\beta}>0$. The block sum is zero while that tail is positive, violating [F2]. Thus $\theta_0$ is outside every fixed polished-tail class.

For a fixed $L\ge1$, take $L_{n_j}=L$ and $K_L=L/\sqrt M$. Since $(1+2p)/(8+8\beta+8p)>0$ and $\rho_j\ge1$, we have $L_{n_j}=L\le K_L\sqrt M\,\rho_j^{(1+2p)/(8+8\beta+8p)}$ for every $j$. Applying [F3] gives $P_{\theta_0}^{(n_j)}\{\theta_0\in\widehat C_{n_j}(L)\}\to0$. By [F6] this is the frequentist coverage at the fixed truth; because $\theta_0\in\Theta_\beta(M)$ by step 1.1, the infimum coverage over that hyperrectangle cannot have lower limit at least $1-\gamma$.

The positive coverage statement [F4] has the additional polished-tail hypothesis, which fails for $\theta_0$ by step 2.1. Thus the sparse-gap undercoverage does not contradict the polished-tail theorem; it refutes only the broader fixed-inflation claim over the full hyperrectangle.

risk_review.notes: Independently checked every local step and the complete published sparse-gap supplier, posterior formula, one-sided bracket and marginal-score proofs. Recursion separates all gaps; the first coordinate is zero, beta>0 makes the truth square-summable, and a positive coordinate after each arbitrarily long zero block defeats every fixed polished-tail inequality. For each fixed L>=1, K_L=L/sqrt(M) meets the exact inflation exponent because M>0 and p>=0. Thus the same fixed truth gives subsequence coverage zero, forcing the hyperrectangle infimum liminf to zero. A>beta and the small-M bound match the supplier; the alpha=0 whole-space branch is excluded on its asymptotic bracket event. The positive polished-tail theorem requires the excluded polished-tail hypothesis and promises conservative rather than exact coverage. Checked primary source arXiv:1310.4489v5 Theorems 3.1 and 3.6 and complete section 9; local endpoint conventions and explicit small-M constants are justified by the local proof rather than attributed verbatim to the paper. Assume AC. Fix $n\ge1$, $p\ge0$, $C\ge1$, a sequence
$C^{-2}i^{-2p}\le\kappa_i^2\le C^2i^{-2p}$, a truth
$\theta_0\in\ell^2(\mathbb N_+,\mathbb R)$, where $\mathbb N_+=\{1,2,\ldots\}$,
and $0<\alpha<\infty$. Consider the prior
$\Pi_\alpha=\bigotimes_{i\ge1}N(0,i^{-1-2\alpha})$ and observations
$X_i=\kappa_i\theta_{0,i}+n^{-1/2}Z_i$, where the $Z_i$ are independent

of the coordinate laws
$$N\!\left( \frac{n\kappa_i x_i}{i^r+n\kappa_i^2}, \frac{1}{i^r+n\kappa_i^2} \right),\qquad i\ge1,$$
For $P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}$-almost every observation $x$, this same kernel is

Let $Q_{n,\alpha}$ be the prior-predictive law of $X$ under this prior and
let $Q_{n,0}=\bigotimes_{i\ge1}N(0,n^{-1})$. Then $Q_{n,\alpha}\ll Q_{n,0}$
and

The same displayed score series also converges absolutely
$P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}$-almost surely; this latter assertion does not identify a
version of the Radon–Nikodym derivative under $P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}$.

Use the Gaussian sequence procedure of
[[def-adaptive-empirical-bayes-gaussian-sequence-procedure]] with fixed
$p\ge0$, $C\ge1$, $A>0$, and
$C^{-2}i^{-2p}\le\kappa_i^2\le C^2i^{-2p}$. Fix $L_0\ge1$, $N_0\ge1$,
$\rho\ge2$, and $\gamma\in(0,1)$. Assume that
$\theta_0\in\Theta_{\mathrm{pt}}(L_0,N_0,\rho)$ and
$\theta_{0,1}=0$. Then there is a finite inflation constant $L>0$,
depending only on the fixed model and class parameters, such that
$$\inf_{\substack{\theta_0\in\Theta_{\mathrm{pt}}(L_0,N_0,\rho)\\ \theta_{0,1}=0}} P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}\{\theta_0\in\widehat C_n(L)\} \longrightarrow1.$$
This is conservative frequentist coverage tending to one, not exact
asymptotic coverage $1-\gamma$. The source also allows a sequence of caps
$A_n>0$ satisfying, for all sufficiently large $n$,
$$A_n\le \frac{\sqrt{\log n}}{4\sqrt{\log(\rho\vee e)}}.$$
In that case there is a constant $K_{\mathrm{infl}}>0$, depending only on the
fixed model and class parameters and not on $n$, such that the same coverage
conclusion holds for any deterministic inflation sequence satisfying
$$L_n\ge K_{\mathrm{infl}}(3\rho^{3(1+2p)})^{A_n}$$
for all sufficiently large $n$.

Use the inverse Gaussian sequence procedure of
[[def-adaptive-empirical-bayes-gaussian-sequence-procedure]] with fixed
$p\ge0$, $C\ge1$, $A>0$, and $\kappa_i^2\in[C^{-2}i^{-2p},C^2i^{-2p}]$.
Fix $L_0\ge1$, $N_0\ge1$, and $\rho\ge2$. Let
$\theta_0\in\Theta_{\mathrm{pt}}(L_0,N_0,\rho)$ with $\theta_{0,1}=0$.
For $n\ge3$ and $\alpha\in[0,A]$, put
$$N_{n,\alpha}=n^{1/(1+2\alpha+2p)},\qquad h_n(\alpha;\theta_0)= \frac{1+2\alpha+2p}{N_{n,\alpha}\log n} \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \frac{n^2 i^{1+2\alpha}(\log i)\theta_{0,i}^2} {(i^{1+2\alpha+2p}+n)^2}.$$
Define
$$\underline\alpha_n= \inf\{\alpha\in[0,A]:h_n(\alpha;\theta_0)\ge(16C^8)^{-1}\}, \qquad \overline\alpha_n= \sup\{\alpha\in[0,A]:h_n(\alpha;\theta_0)\le8C^8\},$$
with the source conventions $\inf\varnothing=A$ and $\sup\varnothing=0$.
Then the source bracket result is
$$\inf_{\theta_0\in\Theta_{\mathrm{pt}}(L_0,N_0,\rho),\,\theta_{0,1}=0} P_{\theta_0}^{(n)} \bigl(\underline\alpha_n\le\widehat\alpha_n\le\overline\alpha_n\bigr) \longrightarrow1.$$
More generally, the same conclusion holds with $A=A_n$ whenever
$$0<A_n\le\frac{\sqrt{\log n}}{4\sqrt{\log(\rho\vee e)}}$$
for all sufficiently large $n$. Uniformly in the polished-tail class, for all sufficiently large $n$,
$$\frac{n^{-2\underline\alpha_n/(1+2\underline\alpha_n+2p)}}{n^{-2\overline\alpha_n/(1+2\overline\alpha_n+2p)}}\le\left[128C^{16}\{4+36L_0\rho^{1+2A_n}\}\right]^{1+2p}.$$
In particular, for fixed $A$ the two rates are uniformly comparable. The lower bracket alone is valid uniformly over arbitrary $\theta_0\in\ell^2$, using the same definition of $\underline\alpha_n$ and the same procedure/domain hypotheses:
$$\inf_{\theta_0\in\ell^2}P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}(\underline\alpha_n\le\widehat\alpha_n)\longrightarrow1.$$

Use the defined inverse Gaussian sequence procedure with fixed $p,C,L_0,N_0,\rho$ and $0<A=A_n\le\sqrt{\log n}/(4\sqrt{\log(\rho\vee e)})$ for all sufficiently large $n$. Write
$$r_\alpha=1+2\alpha+2p,\quad s_\alpha=1+2\alpha,\quad N_\alpha=n^{1/r_\alpha},\quad V_\alpha=N_\alpha\log N_\alpha,\quad f_\alpha(i)=\frac{n^2i^{s_\alpha}\log i}{(i^{r_\alpha}+n)^2},\quad S_\alpha=\sum_i f_\alpha(i)\theta_i^2,\quad h_\alpha=S_\alpha/V_\alpha.$$
The likelihood has a continuous derivative $M_n$ on $[0,A]$, with the derivative at zero interpreted from the right. Let $Q_n=M_n-E_\theta M_n$. Uniformly over $\theta\in\Theta_{\rm pt}(L_0,N_0,\rho)$,
$$E_\theta\sup_{0\le\alpha\le A}\frac{|Q_n(\alpha)|}{V_\alpha(1+h_\alpha)}\le\frac{K\{1+A L_0\rho^{1+2A}\log n\}}{\sqrt{N_A}}\longrightarrow0.$$
For all sufficiently large $n$, all $0\le a\le b\le A$, and every such truth,
$$h_a\le(4+36L_0\rho^{1+2b})\frac{N_b}{N_a}h_b.$$
For every $\theta\in\ell^2$, the expectation satisfies
$$\frac{E_\theta M_n(\alpha)}{V_\alpha}\ge\frac1{8C^4}-C^4h_\alpha,\qquad \frac{E_\theta M_n(\alpha)}{V_\alpha}\le3C^4-C^{-4}h_\alpha.$$
Finally, for arbitrary $\theta\in\ell^2$ and every deterministic interval $[0,c]\subseteq[0,A]$ on which $h_\alpha\le H$, where $H$ is fixed, one has
$$E_\theta\sup_{0\le\alpha\le c}\frac{|Q_n(\alpha)|}{V_\alpha}\le\frac{K_H(1+A\log n)}{\sqrt{N_A}}\longrightarrow0.$$
Constants do not depend on $n,A,\theta$. Fixed finite $A$ is allowed by the eventual cap.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ be a measurable parameter space and, for each integer $n\ge1$, let $\mathcal E_n=((\mathsf Y_n,\mathcal Y_n),(P_{\theta,n})_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a statistical experiment. Let $\Pi_{0,n}$ be a proper prior on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and let $y\mapsto\Pi_n(\cdot\mid y)$ be a supplied posterior probability kernel under the associated prior-predictive law. For $0<\gamma<1$, a data-indexed set rule $C_n:\mathsf Y_n\to\mathcal P(\Theta)$ is a posterior credible set at level $1-\gamma$ if its membership graph $\{(y,\theta):\theta\in C_n(y)\}$ is in $\mathcal Y_n\otimes\mathcal T$ and $\Pi_n(C_n(y)\mid y)\ge1-\gamma$ for every $y$ in its declared data domain. At a fixed truth $\theta\in\Theta$, its frequentist coverage is $c_n(\theta):=P_{\theta,n}\{y:\theta\in C_n(y)\}$. For a truth class $\mathcal T_n\subseteq\Theta$, the rule is asymptotically honest at level $1-\gamma$ on $\mathcal T_n$ if $\liminf_{n\to\infty}\inf_{\theta\in\mathcal T_n}c_n(\theta)\ge1-\gamma$, and it is asymptotically exactly calibrated there if $\sup_{\theta\in\mathcal T_n}|c_n(\theta)-(1-\gamma)|\to0$.

Let $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ be the real square-summable sequence space
from [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]. Fix
$L_0\ge1$, an integer $N_0\ge1$, and $\rho\ge2$. The **polished-tail class**
$\Theta_{\mathrm{pt}}(L_0,N_0,\rho)$ consists of the sequences
$\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ such that for every integer
$N\ge N_0$,
$$\sum_{i=N}^{\infty}\theta_i^2 \le L_0\sum_{i=N}^{\lfloor\rho N\rfloor}\theta_i^2.$$
Thus each tail's total squared mass is controlled by the mass in the finite
block from $N$ through $\lfloor\rho N\rfloor$. The condition concerns block
energy; it is not a coordinatewise upper or lower bound.

derivations.claim: Fix the inflation $L\ge1$ in [F2], depending only on the known constants. Let $B_n=\widehat C_n(L)$, including its whole-space zero-selector branch. With $U=\bigcup_{\beta\in[\beta_-,\beta_+]}\mathcal G_\beta$, [F2] gives $\epsilon_n:=\sup_{\theta\in U}P_\theta^{(n)}\{\theta\notin B_n\}\to0$. This is uniform because $U$ is a subset of the single polished-tail class in that theorem. This step claims conservative coverage only.

The random positive-selector posterior is supported on $\ell^2$ on a single Borel domain, not merely on a separate almost-sure domain for each fixed hyperparameter. Indeed intersect the supplied score domain with $$T_n=\left\{x:\sum_i n^2\kappa_i^2x_i^2/i^2<\infty\right\}.$$ For every square-summable truth the expectation of this nonnegative sum is $$n^2\sum_i\kappa_i^4\theta_i^2/i^2+n\sum_i\kappa_i^2/i^2<\infty.$$ Thus $T_n$ is Borel and has probability one under every such truth. For every $x\in T_n$ and every $a\ge0$, the squared posterior mean is bounded by that same sum, since $i^{1+2a}+n\kappa_i^2\ge i$. For every $a>0$ the variance trace is finite. Hence all positive-parameter posterior laws at these data are supported on $\ell^2$, including the selected law. Extend the selector by zero and use the whole space outside this common declared domain. This changes none of the sampling probabilities and asserts no posterior on the zero branch.

We verify the diameter rate uniformly in $\beta$, rather than import a pointwise Sobolev assertion. Write $q_a=1+2a+2p$, $N_a=n^{1/q_a}$, and $d=\beta-a\ge0$. In the score $h_n(a;\theta)$ of [F3], put $e_i=i^{2\beta}\theta_i^2$, so $\sum_i e_i\le R^2$. For $i\le N_a$, the multiplier of $e_i$ is at most $$\frac{i^{1-2d}\log i}{N_a\log N_a}\le N_a^{-\min(1,2d)}.$$ If $1-2d\ge0$, bound both powers and logarithms by their values at $N_a$; otherwise use $i^{1-2d}\le1$. For $i>N_a$, the multiplier is at most $$\frac{N_a^{2q_a}}{N_a\log N_a}i^{-1-2a-4p-2\beta}\log i\le N_a^{-2d}.$$ The last function of $i$ is decreasing for $i\ge N_a$ once $n$ is uniformly large, since its negative power has exponent at least $1+4p$. Both ranges therefore give $$h_n(a;\theta)\le R^2N_a^{-\min(1,2(\beta-a))}.$$ These bounds hold simultaneously for $0\le a\le\beta$, every $\beta$ in the fixed compact interval, and every $\theta\in\Theta_\beta(R)$.

Choose a fixed $D>0$ with $R^2\exp\{-2D/(1+2\beta_++2p)\}<t$. For all sufficiently large $n$, put $a_{n,\beta}=\beta-D/\log n\ge\beta_-/2$. For every $0\le a\le a_{n,\beta}$, step 1.3 makes $h_n(a;\theta)<t$: here $\min(1,2(\beta-a))\log N_a\ge2D/(1+2\beta_++2p)$ when $\log n\ge2D$. Consequently $\underline\alpha_n\ge a_{n,\beta}$, including the empty-threshold convention $\underline\alpha_n=A$. The uniform lower bracket [F3] yields $$\sup_{\beta,\theta\in\mathcal G_\beta}P_\theta^{(n)}\{\widehat\alpha_n<a_{n,\beta}\}\longrightarrow0.$$ In particular $\delta_n:=\sup_{\theta\in U}P_\theta^{(n)}\{\widehat\alpha_n=0\}\to0$.

Put $H=\{u\in\ell^2:u_1=0\}$, $Z_n=\{\widehat\alpha_n=0\}$ and $E_n=\{\sqrt nX_1\le\Phi^{-1}(1-\gamma)\}$. Define $$C_n=\begin{cases}\ell^2,&Z_n,\\B_n,&Z_n^c\cap E_n,\\B_n\setminus H,&Z_n^c\cap E_n^c.\end{cases}$$ For $n<3$ one may use $\ell^2$. The positive-selector posterior's first-coordinate variance is $(1+n\kappa_1^2)^{-1}>0$, so it assigns $H$ mass zero for every data point of the declared domain, even though the hyperparameter is data-selected. Since $L\ge1$, $B_n$ has posterior mass at least $1-\gamma$; deleting $H$ preserves that mass. On $Z_n$ the specified whole-space convention is retained.

Uniformly for $a\in[\beta_-/2,A]$, split the posterior variance trace at $N_a$. Below that cutoff use $v_i(a)\le C^2i^{2p}/n$; above it use $v_i(a)\le i^{-1-2a}$. Summation and an integral comparison give $$\sum_i v_i(a)\le K n^{-2a/q_a},$$ where $K$ depends only on the fixed constants (the tail factor $1/(2a)$ is uniformly bounded). Markov's inequality applied to the centered posterior squared norm bounds its $(1-\gamma)$ norm quantile by $\sqrt{K/\gamma}\,n^{-a/q_a}$. The variances, hence the norm quantile, decrease with $a$ by coupling all centered coordinates with the same standard normals. On the event of step 2.1, the selected radius is therefore at most $\sqrt{K/\gamma}\,n^{-a_{n,\beta}/q_{a_{n,\beta}}}$. The derivative of $a/q_a$ is $(1+2p)/q_a^2\le1/(1+2p)$, so this is at most $K' n^{-\beta/(1+2\beta+2p)}$ with one $K'$ for the full compact $\beta$ interval. Thus outside an event of uniformly vanishing probability, $\operatorname{diam}(B_n)\le2LK'n^{-\beta/(1+2\beta+2p)}$. This includes the uniformly negligible infinite-diameter zero-selector branch.

This is one rule independent of $\theta$ and $\beta$. Its graph is Borel: the coordinate posterior means and selector are Borel, and the squared norm is the limit of its finite coordinate sums. For completeness, on a fixed countable standard-normal product space the map $(a,z)\mapsto\sum_i v_i(a)z_i^2$ is nonnegative Borel. Integrating its threshold indicators gives a Borel distribution function in $(a,s)$. Its quantile is Borel, by taking the infimum of positive rational radii whose distribution function is at least $1-\gamma$; right continuity ensures this quantile has the required posterior mass. The centered norm has a positive finite quantile: it is finite by its finite second moment and has no atom at zero because its first coordinate is nondegenerate. Thus the radius is positive. Deleting the closed codimension-one hyperplane leaves a dense subset of any positive-radius ball: perturb a point toward the center if necessary and then a sufficiently small amount along the first coordinate. Hence $B_n\setminus H$ has the same diameter $2Lr_{n,\gamma}(\widehat\alpha_n)$ as $B_n$. Diameter is consequently an extended Borel random variable, equal to this expression off $Z_n$ and infinity on $Z_n$.

Every allowed truth lies in $H$ and has $P_\theta^{(n)}(E_n)=1-\gamma$ exactly, since $\theta_1=0$. Its coverage equals $$P_\theta(Z_n)+P_\theta(Z_n^c\cap E_n\cap\{\theta\in B_n\}).$$ Subtracting $P_\theta(E_n)$ leaves $$P_\theta(Z_n\cap E_n^c)-P_\theta(Z_n^c\cap E_n\cap\{\theta\notin B_n\}).$$ Its absolute value is at most $\delta_n+\epsilon_n\to0$ uniformly over both suprema in the question. No independence among $E_n$, the selector and $B_n$ is used. Also $C_n\subseteq B_n$ on every branch, so step 3.1 proves the requested diameter statement, in fact with limiting supremum zero for one sufficiently large fixed diameter constant. The nonzero lower norm bound $m$ is retained and needs no additional argument. This answers the unchanged unrestricted existence question affirmatively. It does not identify the constructed sets as balls or attribute this null-deletion construction to the cited literature.
